entries.title: Kindle Unlimited is now known as Amazon Kinde+
entries.summary: Amazon has shifted away from the Kindle Unlimited name and rebranded it as Kindle+. This change went live today, breaking news. The post Kindle Unlimited is now known as Amazon Kinde+ first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon Kindle Unlimited has just undergone its first major brand shift and will now be known as Kindle+. Amazon rebranded the service to better reflect its growing library, which now extends far beyond e-books to include audiobooks, magazines, and comics.

The biggest update alongside the name change is the deep inclusion of audiobooks. Millions of US subscribers can now read the ebook or listen to the audiobook version at no extra cost. The “+” alignment matches modern streaming services and pairs naturally with Amazon’s existing Audible subscription structure. The core mechanics remain identical. You can still borrow up to 20 titles at a time with no due dates. You can read or listen across any device using the free Kindle App, Kindle e-Reader, or Alexa Tablet.

Amazon has changed the naming convention on all major Kindle+ landing pages from Kindle Unlimited. They also updated the banner image at the top of the screen. The text that outlines the key selling points has also been adjusted to reflect Kindle+

The subscription remains separate from Amazon Prime and costs $11.99 USD per month in the United States; the price may differ in your country. Visit the new Kindle+ page today to buy a membership.

entries.title: Cutting the Cost of Digital Reading
entries.summary: Reading should always be a highly accessible and relaxing escape from reality. It should never transform into a hidden source of lingering financial stress The post Cutting the Cost of Digital Reading first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Digital reading has changed the way we consume literature forever. You can carry an entire library in your pocket wherever you go. The convenience is just unmatched. You can finish a book at midnight, bathed in the soft glow of your screen, and immediately start the sequel without ever leaving your bed.

You have probably looked at your monthly book spending and realized it completely rivals your grocery bill. That same convenience often leads to unexpected expenses. One-tap purchases feel almost invisible at the exact moment of the transaction. You click a single button, and the book appears instantly on your device. And before you realize it, the cost really adds up. Digital storefronts are specifically designed to make spending effortless. Finding a healthy balance between your deep love for books and your long-term financial health is entirely possible. It just requires a mindful shift in how you acquire and manage your digital library. You can read endlessly without completely draining your savings.

Auditing Your Digital Library Habits

The first critical step to reducing your reading costs is understanding exactly where your money goes. Honestly, we are so quick to ignore those digital microtransactions. Storefronts are carefully designed to remove all friction from the buying process. This makes it incredibly easy to spend twenty or thirty dollars a week without noticing the cumulative impact on your wallet. You need to pull back the curtain on those expenses immediately. Start by reviewing your bank statements for the last three to six months. Tally up every single digital book purchase across all your devices and accounts.

The final number might completely surprise you. I guess we all tend to underestimate our small daily habits.

Once you have a crystal-clear picture of your average spending, you can establish a realistic and healthy limit. This is where external tracking tools become incredibly useful for maintaining discipline. You might consider using a free budget app to set a strict monthly allowance for digital literature. By dedicating a specific category to your reading hobby, you eliminate the guilt of purchasing while keeping your overall finances strictly intact. Tracking forces you to be highly intentional with your choices. You stop buying random books you will never actually read, and you start prioritizing the titles you truly want to spend time with. The psychological relief of knowing exactly what you can spend is truly remarkable. The goal is not to stop buying books entirely. The goal is to make sure every dollar spent brings actual value to your reading life.

Maximizing Public Resources

Most local public libraries have fully adapted to the modern digital age. They offer vast collections of electronic books and audiobooks at absolutely no cost to cardholders. You really do not need to own a copy of a book you will only read once. You just need to connect your local library card to their preferred digital lending application on your phone or tablet. The selection often rivals major retail platforms in both quality and quantity. You can find current bestsellers along with sweeping historical biographies and highly popular fiction.

But there is a catch.

The only real drawback is the wait time for heavily requested new titles. You know, waiting can actually build a sense of eager anticipation. You can easily manage this minor inconvenience by keeping a robust and diverse wishlist. Place holds on several different books at the exact same time. As you finish one title, another usually becomes available right on schedule. This rotating system provides a constant stream of new reading material. Another beautiful thing about digital library loans is that they return themselves automatically. You never have to worry about accumulating late fees if you forget to return a book on time. You can also look into non-resident library programs. Some major metropolitan libraries allow non-residents to access their expansive digital catalogs for a small annual fee. This fee is often less than the retail cost of three new digital books. It expands your borrowing options exponentially and drastically reduces your reliance on retail storefronts.

Evaluating Subscription Services Carefully

The digital reading market is completely saturated with unlimited monthly subscription models. These services charge a flat recurring rate for access to a massive catalog of rotating books. But you need to sit down and calculate if these services actually save you money in the long run. A subscription makes perfect sense if you consume five or more books a month consistently. However, it becomes a hidden financial drain if you only read occasionally or go through reading slumps. We all have those months where life gets too busy for reading.

Review the specific catalogs of these services deeply before committing your payment information. Many platforms heavily prioritize independent authors or older catalog titles. They might not carry the latest highly anticipated releases from major traditional publishing houses. You have to ensure the available content actually aligns with your specific daily reading tastes. A great financial strategy is to rotate your active subscriptions throughout the year. You can subscribe to one service for a single month to read the exclusive titles you want, and then immediately cancel the renewal. You can switch to a completely different platform the following month. This active management prevents you from paying for dormant subscriptions that you are not actively utilizing. Sometimes it feels like these companies just hope you forget you are subscribed.

Exploring Public Domain Archives

Classic literature is entirely free if you simply know where to look online. Books published before a certain historical year automatically enter the public domain. Numerous dedicated digital archives offer thousands of these timeless works at zero cost to the public. You can download properly formatted files that work perfectly on your preferred digital reading device.

You can explore the foundational pillars of modern literature without spending a single dime.

This is the perfect way to read those dense classics you have always meant to tackle. You get to expand your literary horizons and protect your budget simultaneously. Many of these archives are beautifully maintained by volunteers who care deeply about making literature accessible to everyone. Taking advantage of these historical resources connects you to the past without costing you anything in the present.

Leveraging Independent Author Promotions

Independent authors frequently use promotional pricing to reach new audiences. They often offer the first book of a long series completely for free. They use this generous strategy to build a dedicated and loyal readership over time. You can sign up for daily newsletters curated by these authors or general digital deal aggregators.

These emails deliver highly discounted or completely free digital books directly to your inbox every single morning. You discover exciting new genres and support emerging independent writers while firmly protecting your wallet. And that is the point, really. It requires a bit of daily sorting through emails, but the reward is a constantly growing digital library built for pennies on the dollar. You might even find your next favorite author before they hit the mainstream bestseller lists. It feels incredibly rewarding to support an unknown writer who eventually finds massive success.

Utilizing Family Sharing Plans

Family sharing plans are another incredible way to cut down your reading expenses. Major digital retailers often allow you to link multiple accounts under a single household umbrella. This means you can share your purchased books with your family members without paying for the exact same title twice. If you have a partner or a sibling with similar reading tastes, pooling your resources is a highly logical step.

You can split the cost of new releases down the middle. This strategy effectively cuts your digital book budget in half right away. It also encourages fun discussions about the books you are both reading at the same time. Maybe you just need to establish some ground rules about who buys what to avoid accidental duplicate purchases.

Conclusion

Reading should always be a highly accessible and relaxing escape from reality. It should never transform into a hidden source of lingering financial stress. You can maintain a vibrant and diverse digital library by simply changing a few of your daily digital habits. Tracking your spending carefully and utilizing your public library resources will dramatically reduce your overall reading costs. You just have to be willing to wait patiently for library holds or explore unfamiliar independent authors. The fundamental joy of getting lost in a great story remains exactly the same. It is a beautiful comfort to know your bank account will simply look much healthier at the end of every month.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: Should Amazon Kindle e-readers have a USB Cable?
entries.summary: Amazon has completely removed the USB-C charging cable from the box for its newest 13th-generation 2026 Kindle family. The post Should Amazon Kindle e-readers have a USB Cable? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The 13th generation line of Kindle e-readers was the first to not include a USB-C cable inside the box. This includes the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Colorsoft, the various Signature Editions, and the models with an aluminum back plate. Even the bundles with a wall charger and case don’t include a charging cable. Given that prices have jumped from $30 to $60 this generation compared to the 12th generation, not including a charging cable really seems like Amazon is nickel-and-diming customers.

If you just opened a newly released 2026 model—such as the base Kindle, the Ube or Graphite, the Kindle Aluminum, or the upcoming Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft models—the packaging intentionally includes only the e-reader and a quick start guide. Amazon has updated its official product pages with a straightforward notice indicating that a USB-C charging cable is not included in the package. The company anticipates that most shoppers already have several compatible cables on hand.

The text is displayed under the different color options of a Kindle e-reader and the bullet-point text breakdown of all of the major selling features. There is a box that says, ” We want you to know: Compatible with a standard USB-C cable. USB-C charging cable is not included in the box. If you need a USB-C cable, you can find one here. Wi-Fi and an Amazon account are required to set up your Kindle and download books.

Amazon now sells an official USB-C to USB-C cable on its website, first available on October 1st, 2026. It costs $4.99 in the United States and a whopping $16.99 in Canada. However, if you purchased a 13th-generation Signature Edition, such as the Paperwhite Signature or Colorsoft Signature, you can bypass cables entirely by using a compatible wireless charging dock or pogo-pin dock accessory.

Do you think Amazon should include a USB-C cable in the box, or do you think everyone who buys one already has multiple cables at home and doesn’t need any additional ones?

Amazon Official USB-C to USB-C Cable for Fire Tablets & other compatible Amazon devices

  • Designed for use with Amazon devices and adapters – With USB-C connectors on both ends, this cable is ideal for fast charging up to 36W and transferring data. (Adapters sold separately.)
  • Lightweight and sleek design that complements the Amazon devices.
  • Easy to store – 3 foot (1 meter) long soft-touch finish that's easy to coil, carry and store.

entries.title: Do you use Storygraph on Kobo e-readers?
entries.summary: Storygraph has been live on Rakuten Kobo e-readers for over five months. Are people actually using it? The post Do you use Storygraph on Kobo e-readers? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Rakuten Kobo announced its integration with StoryGraph in June 2026. Kobo users can enjoy a seamless, automated reading experience that keeps their digital library and reading stats perfectly in sync—at no additional cost.

StoryGraph is a reading tracker and book recommendations app that helps you choose your next read based on your mood and your favorite topics and themes. Founded in 2019, StoryGraph has grown into a global community of over 5 million readers who use the platform to log books, track progress, set reading goals, and find their next great read. With detailed stats, personalized recommendations, book clubs, buddy reads, giveaways, and community challenges, StoryGraph offers a rich, ad-free experience for readers who want to understand their reading lives more deeply. Available on the web, iOS, and Android, StoryGraph was a recipient of a 2025 Apple App Store Award.

The community and media reception to the Kobo and StoryGraph integration—which officially launched on June 29, 2026—has been overwhelmingly positive but mixed with clear feature requests. As the first major e-reader brand to introduce a native, automatic progress sync with an independent book tracker, Rakuten Kobo scored a significant victory over Amazon’s Kindle ecosystem, which remains strictly locked into Goodreads. Readers are thrilled that the integration applies to library books borrowed through Libby via OverDrive, alongside Kobo Store purchases and Kobo Plus subscriptions.

However, there is no support for sideloaded Books added manually with Calibre; PDFs and third-party EPUB files do not sync. This is the #1 complaint from the e-reader community. Progress only flows from Kobo to StoryGraph. Changing your progress on the StoryGraph app will not update your e-reader.

With that in mind, do Rakuten Kobo e-reader owners actually use StoryGraph?

entries.title: Onyx Boox V4.3 software update available soon
entries.summary: This update introduces a variety of multitasking, productivity, and artificial intelligence features designed to make e-reading and note-taking smoother. The post Onyx Boox V4.3 software update available soon first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Onyx Boox Firmware V4.3 software update was officially announced and began rolling out in late October 2026. This update introduces a variety of multitasking, productivity, and artificial intelligence features designed to make e-reading and note-taking smoother.

Onyx BOOX is rolling out this software update for all models released from 2024 to 2026. Onyx confirmed with Good e-Reader that devices three years old will still receive software updates, but once a device reaches EOL, it will no longer be supported.

New Features in Firmware V4.3

• Dual Notes: You can now open, compare, and edit two different notebooks at the same time in either vertical or horizontal split-screen view. You can also use the Lasso tool to drag and drop content between them.

• Talk Insights: This tool allows you to record audio, transcribe it directly to text, translate it, and automatically generate meeting minutes.

• Notes Integration: A new Quick Access panel has been added to let you view and link different notes instantly.

• New Gesture Shortcuts: A two-finger tap will undo your last action, while a three-finger tap will redo it.

• Calendar Memo Enhancements: On 6.13″ Palma devices, the app has been expanded to support 7 writing brushes, the Lasso tool, and general writing capabilities.

• Custom Screensavers: You can now display your current book cover as your screensaver or choose transparent sticker styles.

• Stylus Customization: If your stylus has a physical side button, you can now customize it to trigger shortcuts like the Marker, Eraser, or Lasso tool.

entries.title: Unboxing the new 2026 Amazon Kindle in Ube
entries.summary: This is our comprehensive First Look at the 2026 Amazon Kindle e-reader in Ube. Get a sense of the resolution, specs, and real-world performance. The post Unboxing the new 2026 Amazon Kindle in Ube first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle in Ube is a soft purple edition of the entry-level 6-inch e-reader. Released as part of Amazon’s redesigned 2026 lineup, this version features a lightweight plastic build with a matte finish. Functionally, it stands out with a modern flush-screen, bezel-less design, a 300 PPI display, and 30% faster book opening.

The base Kindle 2026 model has a 1072×1448 resolution and 300 PPI. It has a front-lit display with an adjustable lighting system, and the brightness can be controlled with a slider bar. It has system-wide dark mode that inverts the text to white on a black background, but you can read normally with a white background and black text. The housing is made from recycled materials, and the battery is 100% recycled cobalt. It starts at $149.99 and is available in Ube and Graphite.

The Kindle has 16GB of storage for your e-books and audiobooks. Bluetooth is available to connect wireless headphones to listen to audio content. You can import your Audible collection on the Kindle or buy titles individually from Audible or Amazon. It has Wi-Fi 5 to connect to the internet, buy books, and surf the web with the built-in browser. It is powered by a 1040 mAh battery, which should last about six weeks. It measures 15.28×10.8×0.685 cm and weighs 140 g.

This review video covers the Ube body color, a soft purple. Why did Amazon use this color for the 13th generation? The Ube is a rich purple named after the Filipino purple yam—as part of Amazon’s design shift to introduce playful, food-inspired colorways following the popularity of its earlier Matcha-colored models.

I have been using the new Kindle 2026 in Graphite and have found that page turns happen faster than on the previous generation. It fits in the back of my pocket, which Amazon calls pocket-friendly; however, women tend to have smaller pockets than guys. However, I tend to carry it in my small messenger bag and pull it out at appointments. So far, I have used the new Kindle for about a week, since Amazon sent me the Kindle Paperwhite and the new Kindle Colorsoft, which we will all review soon.

Amazon Kindle 16GB (newest model), Now thinner, lighter, and faster, 6" display, Without Lockscreen...

  • The redesigned Kindle — Now thinner, lighter, faster. New edge-to-edge color and a sleeker, 6" front display. Books open 30% faster vs. the previous Kindle.
  • Up to 6 weeks on a single charge — The display only uses power when you turn the page or use the front light.
  • Easy on the eyes — Read comfortably in bright sunlight or at night on a high-contrast, glare-free display with adjustable brightness.

entries.title: Pocketbook Verse and Verse Lite now have Overdrive Libby
entries.summary: The Pocketbook Verse and Pocketbook Verse Lite now have OverDrive Libby for borrowing e-books from the public library. The post Pocketbook Verse and Verse Lite now have Overdrive Libby first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Pocketbook Verse and the Pocketbook Verse Lite now have OverDrive Libby for borrowing e-books, and magazines from the public library. These devices run firmware 6.11+ and have this functionality built in. Users can browse their local branch’s digital content, check out, and read directly on the e-reader without using a computer. These two e-readers do not have Bluetooth, so you can’t borrow audiobooks.

What’s New​

PocketBook x Libby arrives as a built-in app. Find your library by name, postcode or city (with a country filter), preview titles, or sign in with a library card to borrow. Borrowed e-books open offline in the regular reader; audiobooks stream online. Holds, loan management and early returns are all in the app, along with a shelf for current loans and a menu for switching libraries or cards.

The Task Manager is redesigned. Open apps now appear as cards over whatever is on screen, with shortcuts for Flight mode, Lock, Screenshot and Power off. You can switch between thumbnail and icon views (the choice sticks), apps are sorted by recent use and can be closed from there, and a tap outside or a swipe up dismisses it.

Misc Changes

  • Marker-based text selection in EPUB2 and EPUB3 is fixed — highlights that wouldn’t start, jumped, vanished, spilled across lines, or missed the last characters of a paragraph
  • Dropbox sign-in now works with two-factor authentication enabled
  • Browser gets a newer web engine, plus a fix for sites that didn’t display properly and for cookie-consent choices that weren’t saved
  • Updated system framework for security and compatibility

entries.title: What is Kindle Mode on the new Alexa Tablets?
entries.summary: What is Kindle Mode, which is available on all new Amazon Alexa Tablets? We break down all of the new features and what they do. The post What is Kindle Mode on the new Alexa Tablets? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
A few weeks ago, Amazon announced a new line of tablets called Alexa. They have Android 16 and have full access to the Google Play Store. This is the first time Amazon has done this; in the past, it ran FireOS and only had the Amazon App Store, which lacked mainstream apps. One feature on Alexa tablets is called Kindle Mode; what is it, and what does it do?

Kindle Mode

Kindle Mode activates automatically whenever you open a book inside the native Kindle app. The moment you exit your book or close the app, the tablet immediately reverts to its normal Android tablet interface and standard display settings. When you enter Kindle Mode, the system triggers several background changes designed to mimic a dedicated e-reader

The first new thing that Kindle Mode provides is a distraction-free sanctuary: It silences and mutes all incoming notifications automatically so you can focus entirely on your book. It reduces blue light; the screen shifts to a lower, warmer color temperature that is much softer on the eyes. It limits background processes, stretching the tablet’s battery life up to 20 hours of continuous reading.

One of the standout features is called display profiles. You can customize the look to match your reading material, switching between a classic grayscale look (simulating traditional paper), a soft muted color layout, or a vivid glossy profile suited for magazines and comics.

Kindle Mode is only compatible with the new Amazon Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon Alexa Tablet 11, and Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. Android Police wrote an excellent article on how to replicate it on Samsung Galaxy tablets.

Up to 16 hours of video playback, quad speakers and Dolby Atmos, Wi-Fi 6E, 13MP rear camera, and 8MP front camera.

entries.title: Amazon Kindle Oasis back in stock in the United States
entries.summary: The Amazon Kindle Oasis is back in stock on Amazon for a limited time. They are used and reasonably priced. The post Amazon Kindle Oasis back in stock in the United States first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle Oasis is back in stock for a limited time on the main Amazon.com website in the United States. The Graphite model with 8GB of storage is $115, the Oasis Graphite model with 32GB of storage is $145, and the Champagne Gold model with 32GB is $144. These prices are very good; considering the last time the 8GB model was in stock, it cost over $178.00.

All Kindle Oasis models that are back in stock are used, this means they are returned or a trade-in for a newer model. The Oasis remains one of Amazon’s most-regarded e-readers because it was the last to have physical page-turn buttons.

The Kindle Oasis 3 features a 7-inch E Ink Carta HD capacitive touchscreen display with a resolution of 1680 x 1264 and 300 PPI. The screen is glass, and the body is high-grade aluminum. It has a front-lit display and is the first Kindle with a color temperature system. The front-lit display and color system can both be controlled by slider bars in the quick settings menu, or can automatically be adjusted based on the time of day via the ambient light sensor. It has 25 LED lights total, 12 white and 13 amber.

Underneath the hood is a Freescale/NXP IMX7 dual-core 1 GHZ processor with 512 MB of RAM. The Oasis keeps the two manual page-turn buttons on the right side of the screen, and the settings menu lets you reverse the page turns, so up is down and down is up, which is ideal for manga. This is the only Kindle model that has physical page turn buttons. If you hold the e-reader in one hand while reading an ebook, you can disable the touchscreen; this is useful on public transit.

If you love reading in the bathtub or at the beach, the Kindle Oasis 3 is waterproof. It is certified IPX8 to protect against immersion in up to two meters of freshwater, for up to 60 minutes. If your Kindle is splashed with water, wipe it off with a soft cloth and keep on reading. If your Kindle is immersed in water, remove its cover, make sure no cables are plugged into the device, and do not attempt to charge your Kindle until it is completely dry. If your Kindle is immersed in salt water, chlorinated water, soapy water, or liquids other than fresh water, make sure you rinse that liquid out of the device with fresh water such as cold tap water. Then dry your Kindle.

Kindle Oasis – With 7” display and page turn buttons

  • Our best 7", 300 ppi flush-front Paperwhite display.
  • Adjustable warm light to shift screen shade from white to amber.
  • Waterproof (IPX8) so you can read in the bath or by the pool. Your Kindle has been tested to withstand accidental immersion in water.

entries.title: All of the new 2026 Kindles have user replaceable batteries
entries.summary: All of the new 2026 Amazon Kindle e-readers made of plastic or aluminum have user-replaceable batteries. Battery Health can be viewed in the settings menu, and a QR code takes you to battery replacements. The post All of the new 2026 Kindles have user replaceable batteries first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
All of the latest-generation Amazon Kindle e-readers have user-replaceable batteries. This includes the new Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Colorsoft, and the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition. There is this new Amazon Kindle Battery Guide page that was recently added to the help section of Amazon’s website.

With Amazon’s freshly redesigned 2026 Kindle lineup, replacing the battery has become significantly easier. Driven by upcoming European Union regulations, Amazon built these models with a removable, user-replaceable back panel (EBR-compliant), entirely shifting away from the tightly glued-shut designs of previous generations. Depending on whether you have a standard plastic model or an upgraded aluminum variant, accessing and swapping the battery differs slightly.

The plastic models tend to pop off very easily, since there are no screws. All you need is your fingernail, a guitar pick, or something similar. Remove the battery by unscrewing the four Phillips-head screws securing it to the frame. On Kindles with an aluminum backplate, remove two tiny hex screws on the bottom edge of the device. Then pry it open with a fingernail, guitar pick, or something similar.

View battery health

The 2026 Amazon Kindle e-readers all have a new battery health system. You can check your device’s current health directly by navigating to Settings > Device options > Battery > Battery information. The device will flag if it is running normally, has limited capacity, or recognizes an incompatible third-party cell. Amazon includes QR codes directly within the device firmware interface that link to approved battery replacement kits and official replacement instructions.
